opus-5.5.text:
I think we have to be honest with ourselves here. There's a big gap between what you see in a demo video and what it takes for a robot to actually show up every day and do a job reliably. A lot of the promises right now are being made on the strength of the demo, not the deployment.

When I think about whether a robot can be a "productive employee," I look at a few things. First, success rate. A demo might succeed once out of ten tries, and you only see the one. In a factory or a pharmacy or a warehouse, if the robot fails even a few percent of the time and needs a human to come rescue it, the economics fall apart. You haven't replaced labor, you've just created a new babysitting job.

Second, generalization. Can it handle the object it's never seen, the box that's slightly crushed, the lighting that changed, the shelf that got rearranged? That's where most systems still struggle, because data for embodied intelligence is extremely scarce compared to language or images. Teleoperation data is expensive and slow to collect. That's why in our work we've put so much emphasis on large-scale synthetic data and simulation, so the model has seen millions of variations before it ever touches the real world, and then we use a smaller amount of real data to close the gap.

Third, speed and cost. If a robot is reliable but works at a third of human speed and costs more than the worker it's replacing, it's still a research project, not an employee.

So my view is: the direction is right, and I'm very optimistic about it, but we should start with scenarios that are closed enough and valuable enough, things like retail shelves, pharmacies, picking in logistics, where the robot can genuinely run a full shift and create value. Prove it there, then expand. If the industry promises a general-purpose household butler next year, I think that's going to disappoint people and hurt the whole field. The companies that win will be the ones that are actually counting the hours robots work unassisted, not the views on their videos.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd separate the promise into two layers, because people tend to blur them together.

The first layer is whether a robot can perform a task in a demo. That bar has gotten remarkably low. With teleoperation data, a well-tuned policy, and a controlled scene, you can get a humanoid to fold a towel or sort objects, and the video looks fantastic. I take almost nothing from those videos. Not because they're fake, but because they answer a question nobody actually needs answered.

The second layer is whether the robot can do that task a thousand times, in a factory or a warehouse that wasn't arranged for it, with lighting that changes, with objects it hasn't seen, and when it fails, fail in a way that doesn't stop the line or hurt someone. That's what "employee" means. An employee is defined by reliability and generalization, not by a best-case run. And on that layer, I think we're honestly still early. The gap between 90 percent success and 99.9 percent success is not a matter of scaling a bit more; it's where most of the real research problems live.

So when I hear a company say they'll deploy thousands of robots as workers in a year or two, the questions I ask are very practical. What's the success rate over a long horizon, not a single pick? How much of the environment had to be modified to make it work? Is there a human in the loop, and if so, how many robots per human? What happens when the robot encounters something outside the training distribution? If a company can answer those with numbers, I take them seriously. If the answer is another video, I don't.

I'd also say I'm not pessimistic about the direction. The data flywheel is real, the models are genuinely getting more general, and the cost of hardware is coming down fast. My disagreement is mostly about timelines and about the honesty of the framing. I think we'll see robots doing narrow, structured jobs well within a few years. The general-purpose employee that walks into any workplace and just starts working, I think that's a longer story than the current fundraising cycle would suggest.

astra-6.text:
I would separate a compelling demonstration from a productive employee. In a demonstration, you can choose the task, prepare the environment, and show the best run. In a workplace, the robot has to keep delivering useful results when conditions change.

So I’d ask: How often does it succeed? How much human intervention does it need? And what is the cost per completed task once you include installation, maintenance, and downtime? If someone has to stand nearby and rescue it every few minutes, you haven’t really automated the work.

I’m optimistic, but I would judge each promise against a specific job. Moving the same objects between two stations is very different from doing whatever a warehouse worker might encounter during a shift. The strongest evidence is sustained performance in a customer’s actual operation—and whether that customer wants to buy more.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d judge those promises by what the robot can reliably do, rather than what it can do once in a demonstration. Can it finish a useful task repeatedly, handle variations, and recover when something goes wrong? How much human supervision does it need? And does the value of the work justify the full cost of operating it?

A robot can look very impressive in a short video while still being a long way from a productive employee. The important step is sustained performance in a real workplace. I’m optimistic about the potential, but I’d want to see that evidence before accepting a broad promise.
